newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqis slaughter sheep for Saddam at oil station.
newsitem.headline: Iraqis slaughter sheep for Saddam at oil station.

text.p: Farmers slaughtered sheep under the feet of Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein on Tuesday as he elbowed his way through a huge crowd into the control room of Iraq's oil pipeline to Turkey.

Journalists and Iraqi ministers had to wait three hours by a maze of pipelines at the Number One pumping station in Kirkuk for Saddam's arrival to unleash Iraqi crude oil to world markets for the first time in more than six years.
School children broke into shouts of "Hala bik hala" (You are most welcome) as Saddam appeared at the site.
"We shall sacrifice our blood and soul for you, Saddam," a crowd of several thousand civil servants and farmers from nearby villages chanted.
The 59-year-old president, dressed in field marshal uniform, looked confident and relaxed.
He smiled as he pressed the button to set the oil running through the twin pipeline and chuckled when reporters asked him to make a statement.

"In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate, we open our eternal project, the northern oil...We pray the Almighty...to maintain for the Iraqis the blessing of stability and great gains and achieve one victory upon another for them," Saddam said.
(In Ankara, a Turkish oil official said no Iraqi oil had arrived at Turkey's Ceyhan terminal hours after Iraq said it had begun pumping crude from Kirkuk.)
Kirkuk, 300 km (190 miles) north of Baghdad, is the hub of the oil industry in northern Iraq and where oil was first struck in Iraq in 1927.
There were shouts of "Allahu Akbar" (God is Greatest) from the crowd after Saddam's remarks. Many people including two high-ranking officials burst into tears.
"God put an end to our pain. We have suffered a lot," said one man. Among the children in the crowd, several wore torn shoes. Some emaciated children shivered from cold.

Iraq is under crippling U.N. trade sanctions for invading Kuwait in 1990. The embargo which includes a ban on oil exports permits imports of food and medicine but Iraq has run out of ready cash to pay for them.
The United Nations on Monday gave Iraq clearance to start limited oil exports from Tuesday to allow it to raise funds to buy food, medicine and other humanitarian items for Iraqis.
The oil-for-food deal, signed in May, allows oil exports worth $2 billion over six months.
U.N. relief agencies in Baghdad say about 4,500 Iraqi children die a month for lack of food and medicine and more than half a million children are severely malnourished.

"There has been enough hardship, enough agony to the Iraqi people. These sanctions are fully unjustified and we are waiting desperately...for pumping oil," Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed told reporters.
